subject: Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts: I just had the head-smacking experience of being frustrated with a poorly sampling model only to discover that I had a parameter defined that I never actually used (relic from an earlier more complicated model). Presumably it wouldn't be too difficult to add a check before compilation for this sort of thing?

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
Let's say we have the following stan code:

    data{
        int<lower=1> N ;
        vector[N] Y ;
    }
    parameters{
        real mu ;
        real sigma ;
    }
    model{
        Y ~ normal(mu,1)
    }

The parameter sigma is never actually used. Maybe it was at some point during model development but then the user decided to hard-code the SD of the gaussian to 1 for some reason, but forgot to take out sigma. Presumably it should be relatively trivial to use simple string searches before compilation to check for variables that are initialized but then never appear in any sampling or transforms.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
Andrew's also been asking us to start providing
lint-like warnings.

This is a good one --- our C++ compilers warn us when
we have an unused variable.

It's possible with the current Stan to C++ translation
pipeline, which produces an abstract syntax tree
intermediate representation. That tree can be
walked and searched for variables, expression types,
functions, etc.

The complicated part is dealing with the Boost
variant types, which require a callback structure
rather than the usual kind of programming. There
are lots of examples to follow.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
It's surprisingly tricky to do this right with string search.
There are quoted strings, substrings, operators and functions,
comments, declaration and use scope, and identifier
type.

Having said that, it'd be really great to build something
along the lines of Google's cpplint program, which we
use ourselves. It's a Python program that runs over
C++ code looking for various kinds of coding problems.
You can get pretty far with string matching and also
detect other kinds of problems.

- Bob

messages.author: 4e90fa9f1b035969
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
Just ran into a similar problem with unused transformed parameters. In the process of modifying a model I ended up with something like: 

data {
  int n;
}
parameters {
  vector[n] x;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[n] foo;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(0, 1);
}

Which samples, but returns an error only after sampling (which takes ~3 days in my case):

Error in validObject(.Object) : 
  invalid class “stanfit” object: The following variables have undefined values:  foo[1],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[2],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[3],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[4],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[5]...

 Maybe this has already been proposed elsewhere, but it might be worth raising a warning or error when checking or compiling a model if a *transformed* parameter is declared but never assigned a value or used. I can't think of an instance when I would want to declare a transformed parameter but never assign value(s) to it, but I could be overlooking a case where this would be useful.

You can get pretty far with string matching and also
detect other kinds of problems.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
On Wednesday, March 22, 2017 at 10:56:59 AM UTC-4, Maxwell Joseph wrote:
 I can't think of an instance when I would want to declare a transformed parameter but never assign value(s) to it, but I could be overlooking a case where this would be useful.

It can be useful when there's the possibility of a zero-length transformed parameter. For example, 

data {
 ...
 int<lower=0,upper=1> flag;
}
...
transformed parameters {
  real x[flag];
  if (flag) {
    // do something with x only if flag==1
  }
}

Other than the zero-length case I can't think of any reason to declare a transformed parameter and never assign anything to it.

messages.author: 4e90fa9f1b035969
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
Ah - I can see that being useful. Maybe I can clarify what my problem was. 

In your example, there is possibly something being assigned to x within that conditional statement, depending on the value of flag. 

My mistake was that there was no possibility of assignment anywhere (not even in a conditional statement) - just a declaration at the beginning of the transformed parameter block. This seems like it may be a separate (mis)use case.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
parts:
If you declare a transformed param and don't assign to it, it should
have a NaN value (which would violate any constraint, but be OK in
the unconstrained case). Where does the problem arise? Are you trying
to use it in generated quantities?

We could probably stand to check even the unconstrained values aren't
NaN. It's hard to know what to do in some of these cases because we
don't want to mess with the underlying IEEE numerics more than we need
to and none of those crash when fed NaN---they just keep returning NaN.
But some of our functions from Boost and that we wrote themselves, will
throw exceptions.

We do suggest always running a few real iterations before setting things
off for days.

- Bob
